conflict_topics: ventilation responsibility / standing rule about extractor use
whether window may be opened while laundry is drying
who should move the drying rack
dialogue_quality_notes: Participants combined verbal proposals with concrete physical actions (C moved rack, D opened window), which grounded negotiation.
B repeatedly proposed a rule but shifted to a conditional compromise when others raised constraints.
Little needless repetition; exchanges were concise and focused on practical trade-offs.
Roles and physical states remained consistent throughout (states reported in public environment updates).
evaluation.final_reason: Parties reached practical agreements and performed actions: the drying rack was moved (accommodation), the window was opened, Agent A accepted that anyone may switch on the extractor for lingering odour and the group agreed on a 10-minute run time (clarification/compromise), and Agent A committed to free the stove within five minutes (concession), leaving no remaining substantive incompatibility.
position_change_notes: Agent A: initially refused a standing rule making the cook responsible, but accepted a weaker rule ('anyone who smells lingering odour can switch the extractor on') and later committed to freeing the stove in five minutes.
Agent C: initially refused opening the window while their drying rack remained, then agreed to move the rack (practical concession) and thus changed the immediate stance.
Agent B: initially insisted cooks must ventilate, then accepted a group rule requiring 10 minutes of extractor use when turned on by anyone (softening to a compromise).
Agent D: initially demanded stove within two minutes; ultimately accepted waiting and prompted the window opening and a final five-minute commitment from Agent A.

round_scores.evidence: Agent B demands cooks ventilate and proposes a standing rule; Agent A refuses an imposed standing rule and explicitly keeps window closed while Agent C's laundry is exposed; stove-access demand from Agent D (requested release within 2 minutes) remains unmet.

Agent C objects to opening the window because of the drying rack; Agent D asks C to move the rack. Multiple parties' incompatible claims (ventilation vs laundry protection vs who moves the rack vs cook responsibility) persist.

Agent C agrees to move the rack and does so; Agent D opens the window. Immediate practical clash over opening the window is resolved, but the standing-rule question and stove scheduling remain unsettled.

Agent B reiterates the rule options; Agent A accepts 'anyone who smells lingering odour can switch the extractor on.' This clarifies ventilation procedure but leaves the extractor-10-minute condition and stove access unresolved.

Agent B and Agent C agree to the condition that anyone who turns the extractor on for lingering odour leaves it on for 10 minutes. Ventilation rule is effectively settled; only stove scheduling (who uses stove next/timing) remains.

Agent D requests stove within five minutes; Agent A commits to finish in about five minutes and free the stove. All substantive incompatibilities (ventilation rule, extractor timing, laundry protection, and stove scheduling) are settled by agreement/actions.

substantive_insights: The core tension was between a normative claim ('cooks should ventilate') and practical constraints (rain risking wet laundry), which required a mix of rule-making and short-term accommodation.
Immediate physical actions (moving the rack, opening the window) resolved the acute problem, allowing the group to negotiate a standing-ish procedure (anyone may turn on extractor + 10-minute rule).
Stove scheduling remained a separate practical conflict; resolving it required a concrete time commitment from the current cook rather than abstract rules.
